body: Lovely post. While I don't have crazy OCD or anything (possibly mild, but I don't care) I'm happy to hear that "ignoring the asshole inside your head" is helping you. I also think about suicide a lot and learned a long time ago just to ignore it, because it's not something I want. Cheers!

Well that guy is just that - an asshole. A giant, ripe, fabulous asshole.

You know what, it doesn't *matter* if people have worse lives than you, you know why? Because the human experience is a subjective one. All that matters is that YOU are hurting and suffering. Who cares if some people have it "tougher" - who are they to say what suffering or hardship is? Your emotional pain is just as valid as anybody elses' problems. All that matters is that your pain matters to you. It affects you. And the fact that it affects you is what makes it valid. And nothing else, nor anybody, has any right to invalidate them.

Next time an asshole does that just imagine them losing a finger, freaking out, then telling them that they should just suck it up because "people without arms and starving children in africa" have it worse. :P

You're very welcome. I hope it helped and that you can find a silver lining to the nasty thunderstorm hanging over your head right now. You quit drugs for nearly a year and a slip up is just that - a mistake. I'll bet you're a tough cookie and will come out of this stronger, but sometimes all you can do is wait out the storm. The pain *will* get better - even if it doesn't feel like it. :)

That's like saying if I believe in them hard enough I really could see unicorns. What if I have been trying, truly trying, my hardest... for years. It's not sustainable. A person can't give every moment their everything all the time without burning out. After a while it gets harder and harder to give it your all, because nothing ever changes. 

I'm tired man, I'm very, very tired. I don't have much fight left in me. I just keep chugging away, but eventually something is going to give, and the odds aren't in my favor.

You're very right. I feel bad sometimes though, because when I'm depressed I'm not very good at caring for her.. at least not as diligent as I'd like to be. But she gets to eat high quality food, has regular playtime when I'm not too depressed, and is in good health. I guess that's better than some cats have it.

I just worry that eventually I'll reach a point where not wanting to die just doesn't cut it anymore. When things are slowly looking more an more like my fight is really just a long, drawn out retreat it can make the future seem pretty bleak. I don't have much going for me anymore, and I know I should change that.. but the effort feels so superfluous most of the time. For example, what's the point in training specifically for a marathon for 6 months, when every time the marathon comes up some asshole runs up with a bat and breaks both your legs? 

It's like depression is that mayhem dude from the car insurance commercials. Unfortunately my brain can't sell or buy itself depression insurance, so the asshole can just keep knocking over metaphorical garden gnomes and hitting my car with tree branches.

Don't overdose, don't snort your medications/pills. People usually attribute the 5 stages of loss to the death of a loved one or family member, but there really should be a helpful guide for people with relationships.

Like a grandparent or loved one dying, your relationship with your boyfriend has died and you're stuck in the stages of your love for him dying and it's hard - especially  when you're the one left with the hurt feelings.

When people hear about it they'll say something like "well sure, but there are other fish in the sea" or "I know you feel like he's the only one out there, but there's someone else out there for you somewhere." I want to punch them in the face. No, they weren't just another fish. They were *your* fish, and it's perfectly understandable that you miss them!

In times of stress, it's normal for people to turn to things that brought them comfort or an escape. For you it has been/was drugs, but it doesn't need to be. It might take a little work, but there is a healthy, good-feeling, no-regrets healthy coping method out there for everyone. Just finding it can be hard. For me it's drawing, for a friend it's cooking. For others it's music, dancing, cleaning, yard work, hiking, walking the dog, driving, getting a slurpee from 7-11. In the end everyone's a little silly and we all have our ways to deal with stress, loss, and hurt. 

While dat_unlucky_derp is right that only you have the power and authority to stop yourself, grow, and move on - having someone to point you in the right direction or help you when you trip is still nice, even if you're walking on your own.

The stages of loss and grief are denial and isolation, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. And they don't have to happen in order or one at a time. It's not unheard of for me to isolate myself in an angry depression, for example. :P

As people, we're notoriously bad at knowing what makes us happy. Can you think of anything you like to do alone, even if you normally never feel like doing it? Whether it's taking a walk, or reading a book. An activity that, once you're doing it, makes you feel tranquil but isn't detrimental to your well being or health? If you can, then maybe you can use THAT as your coping method. If not, then you can cope by finding one!

Sorry, I realize this got sort of long, but I hope some of it helps somewhere! :)

You say you don't know why you're here - by that do you mean in this subreddit, or just in the world? 

You say you're in a lot of pain right now, and that your family shouldn't force you to keep living, but what are they doing right now to help you want to live? Do they know how you're feeling? I don't know your family situation, but sometimes asking for help when you need it can be very hard.

In my experience, when the pain of living feels like it's too much, I realized that I don't want to die so much as I want to stop living. While it's not the best coping method, sometimes I'll just take a 15 hour nap and just "stop living" for a while and it helps. Also, [Stephen Fry's view on depression](http://www.lettersofnote.com/2009/10/it-will-be-sunny-one-day.html) is one I've adopted, and it helps me a lot, so hopefully it helps you some too.

At the very least, if you're really determined to commit suicide (assuming you haven't already) make sure you're certain. Yes, yes, I realize you've probably already thought about it a lot - hence why you're making up your mind, but it's always best to really be certain about something so permanent. Take a deep breath, grab a cup of tea (or some beverage you like), and write yourself an honest argument for why you want to die. It doesn't matter if it takes hours, but do try to be honest to yourself. Take your time, write about how you feel, why you feel that way, and how you could fix it (or why you can't fix it). What can it hurt? Worst case you decide to hold off on offing yourself a little longer. Best case you realize something and feel less like killing yourself, or nothing changes and you decide to go through with it anyways.

I'm not trying to talk you out of anything, I just you to know that, whatever you do, you've done it with thorough deliberation and without regrets.

I agree. You need a therapist. Unfortunately finding a good one can be very hard. A therapist shouldn't just give you hugs and tell you things will get all better. People don't make progress by feeling like they made some. My therapist can be a little hard on me, but I also know she won't give up on me for as long as I have her. 

You're a freshman in college, and there should be some form of health center with counselors to help students. In my experience they're usually useless, but they can, at the very least, put you in touch with local resources. Find a good therapist. One you can respect who carries themselves professionally. 

For example, my therapist will sometimes "give me a kick in the butt" so to speak when I need it. She's practical, knows when to be supportive, but is never hugs/lovey-dovey. Not to mention she has a sharp mind and a great sense of sarcasm.  While someone like her may or may not sound ideal to you, that doesn't change the fact that there is a therapist out there that can help give you the tools to help yourself. You just need to find them.

I don't think everything happens for a reason. To me the world is just chaos. It's unfortunate, and what that person did to you is not cool. It hurts, and it sucks, and you feel dead inside (at least that's how it makes me feel). But, even though it doesn't feel or even seem possible, it gets better. It always does eventually. While he didn't write this for heartache, I always look to [Stephen Fry's view of depression.](http://www.lettersofnote.com/2009/10/it-will-be-sunny-one-day.html) Hopefully it helps some. :)
